name: Support for Tutors and Intervention Groups
title: Support for Tutors and Intervention Groups
answer: This idea is about using AI to support the adults who teach math, especially tutors and teachers running intervention groups, rather than having AI teach students directly. In the book's account, an AI assistant suggests what a tutor might say next, while the tutor keeps the teaching role and adjusts the support. It matters because the text reports that this kind of support improved student mastery, with the largest gains for students of the weakest tutors.

sections.body: The idea addresses a common gap in math support: tutors and intervention teachers need timely guidance about what to do next with each student. The book describes an AI assistant that coaches the tutor by suggesting possible next lines or moves. The tutor remains the person who teaches the child, reads the suggestion, adjusts it, and uses their own judgment. This solves the problem of leaving novice tutors or busy teachers to plan every intervention from scratch. It also gives districts a way to evaluate tutoring services and volunteer training by asking whether the tool supports the tutor or tries to replace them.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In math across kindergarten through 12th grade, the text gives no separate grade bands, so the same pattern applies wherever tutoring or intervention happens. A district or school can provide each tutor with a short brief that summarizes what a student is working on and where they struggle, so the session starts faster. The tutor is the one who reads the brief, makes adjustments, and applies personal judgment during the session. For intervention groups, a teacher can use data from Zearn or Khan Academy to plan the groups, then ask an AI tool to draft a short lesson for each group. The teacher changes the drafted lesson using knowledge of the students, and the time freed up is returned to the small group lessons.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as some of the best evidence for AI in math, specifically evidence about helping the adults who teach it. It describes a large trial in a Southern US school district in which novice tutors working with 1,800 students received an AI assistant that suggested what to say next (Wang et al., 2024). The text reports that students whose tutors had access were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics, and that students of the weakest tutors gained 9 points. The text notes that the study used a research tool rather than a commercial product, so the finding guides district choices rather than endorsing a specific product.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets a clear limit: the tool's job was to coach the tutor, while the tutor remained the one who taught the child. The tutor is the person who reads the brief, adjusts it, and applies their own judgment, so the decision about what to say and do stays with the person. For intervention groups, the teacher changes the AI-drafted lesson using what they know about the students, so the plan is not handed over to the tool. When a district buys tutoring services or trains volunteer tutors, it should seek tools that assist tutors instead of taking their place. The evidence comes from a research tool, not a commercial product, so the text does not promise that any purchased tool will produce the same result.
